question:
In a small pond there are eleven lily pads in a row labeled \(0\) through \(10.\) A frog is sitting on pad \(1.\) When the frog is on pad \(N,\) where \(0 < N < 10,\) it will jump to pad \(N-1\) with probability \(\frac{N}{10}\) and to pad \(N+1\) with probability \(1-\frac{N}{10}.\) Each jump is independent of the previous jumps.

If the frog reaches pad \(0\) it will be eaten by a patiently waiting snake. If the frog reaches pad \(10\) it will exit the pond, never to return. What is the probability that the frog will escape without being eaten by the snake?
solution:
The current pad determines the frog's future jump probabilities, so let \(p_n\) be its probability of eventually escaping when starting on pad \(n\). The endpoint conditions are \(p_0=0\) and \(p_{10}=1\). Splitting according to the next jump gives, for \(1\le n\le9\),
\[
p_n=\frac{n}{10}p_{n-1}+\frac{10-n}{10}p_{n+1}.
\]
To turn these equations into a calculation we can carry from one pad to the next, rearrange them to compare neighboring differences:
\[
(10-n)(p_{n+1}-p_n)=n(p_n-p_{n-1}).
\]
Define \(d_n=p_n-p_{n-1}\) for \(1\le n\le10\). Then
\[
d_{n+1}=\frac{n}{10-n}d_n\qquad(1\le n\le9),
\]
where every denominator is positive. Put \(x=d_1=p_1\). Successive use of the recurrence gives
\[
d_1=x,\quad d_2=\frac{x}{9},\quad d_3=\frac{x}{36},
\]
\[
d_4=\frac{x}{84},\qquad d_5=\frac{x}{126}.
\]
Continuing gives \(d_6=d_5\), \(d_7=d_4\), \(d_8=d_3\), \(d_9=d_2\), and \(d_{10}=d_1\).

When all ten differences are added, the intermediate probabilities cancel. Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
1&=p_{10}-p_0=\sum_{n=1}^{10}d_n\\
&=2x\left(1+\frac19+\frac1{36}+\frac1{84}+\frac1{126}\right)\\
&=\frac{146}{63}x.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the requested probability is \(p_1=x=\boxed{\frac{63}{146}}\), choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
